                                  13
                                              Plaintiff RingCentral, Inc. (“RingCentral”) moves to dismiss defendant AmeriSave
                                  14
                                       Mortgage Corporation’s (“AmeriSave”) amended counterclaim as barred by the claims’ statute of
                                  15
                                       limitations and as inadequately pleaded under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 9(b) and 12(b)(6).
                                  16
                                       It also moves to strike various portions of AmeriSave’s counterclaim, including its request for
                                  17
                                       punitive damages and attorneys’ fees, as well as references to mediation proceedings and
                                  18
                                       RingCentral’s “pattern” of misconduct towards customers. AmeriSave has failed to adequately
                                  19
                                       plead its claims under both Rules 9(b) and 12(b)(6), except for its breach of contract claim.
                                  20
                                       Accordingly, I GRANT RingCentral’s motion to dismiss, with leave to amend. RingCentral’s
                                  21
                                       motion to strike is DENIED; its requests are both premature and speculative.
                                  22
                                                                                BACKGROUND
                                  23
                                          1. Factual Background
                                  24
                                              AmeriSave is a “direct-to-consumer mortgage lender” who “primarily does business with
                                  25
                                       consumers via telephone.” Defendant’s Amended Counterclaim (“AC”) [Dkt. No. 39] at ¶¶ 4, 10.
                                  26
                                       In its view, if “its telephones do not work properly, [AmeriSave] simply cannot conduct its
                                  27
                                       business.” Id. ¶ 10.
                                  28
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO            Document 53        Filed 04/29/26    Page 2 of 17




                                   1          RingCentral is a “provider of cloud communication platforms that include message, video,

                                   2   phone, and contact center services.” Id. ¶ 11. Beginning in March 2021, RingCentral and

                                   3   AmeriSave “entered into discussions regarding whether RingCentral was capable of developing a

                                   4   custom, cloud-based communication platform system for AmeriSave,” as it had done for similar

                                   5   third parties in the past. Id. ¶¶ 12–13. On March 23, 2021, and April 2, 2021, the parties met, and

                                   6   RingCentral “presented to AmeriSave a demonstration of its solution.” Id. ¶ 14. During these

                                   7   demonstrations, “RingCentral, through its executives, represented that it could create a custom,

                                   8   cloud-based communication platform system for AmeriSave that would resolve call quality and

                                   9   scalability issues.” Id. ¶ 16. Based on these representations, AmeriSave entered into a Master

                                  10   Services Agreement (“MSA”) with RingCentral on April 27, 2021. Id. ¶¶ 17, 19.

                                  11          In the six months following the signing of the MSA, AmeriSave describes RingCentral’s

                                  12   “implementation efforts [as] both erratic and incomplete.” Id. ¶ 21. This resulted in AmeriSave
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   incurring “significant costs—including the costs of third-party consultants—to assist in

                                  14   troubleshooting the erratic and incomplete implementation efforts.” Id. ¶ 22. Aware of

                                  15   AmeriSave’s growing frustrations, RingCentral executive Paul Buday “offered to delay charges on

                                  16   related invoices until the product was live.” Id. ¶ 23. Later, on October 20, 2021, Stewart

                                  17   Goldfarb, RingCentral’s Senior Manager of Professional Services, notified AmeriSave that it

                                  18   “couldn’t deliver the calls at a pace necessary to achieve AmeriSave’s business objectives,” and

                                  19   that RingCentral was not able to implement its original plans due to a “fundamental limitation.”

                                  20   Id. ¶¶ 24–25. RingCentral instead offered an alternative proposal—one that would require five

                                  21   additional months—that AmeriSave found “untenable,” as it “would have forced [it] to entirely

                                  22   change its operating structure.” Id. ¶ 25.

                                  23          Recognizing the “untenability” of this proposal, “Goldfarb, with the approval of other

                                  24   RingCentral executives, offered a separate proposal to deploy the completed portion of the system

                                  25   in a phased approach as originally planned, purportedly working to address timeline acceleration

                                  26   and to provide answers to AmeriSave.” Id. ¶ 26. By November 2021, RingCentral executives

                                  27   “continued to lull AmeriSave’s concerns by stating that it was still working on solutions and

                                  28   recommendations to accommodate AmeriSave’s needs.” Id. ¶ 27.
                                                                                        2
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO            Document 53         Filed 04/29/26     Page 3 of 17




                                   1           In December 2021, AmeriSave sent a letter to RingCentral, expressing concerns with its

                                   2   performance. Id. ¶ 28. RingCentral’s Senior Vice President of Legal, Jose Serrano, responded,

                                   3   indicating that “RingCentral and its senior executives were committed to delivering a system to

                                   4   AmeriSave and working toward an amicable resolution for the Parties.” Id. During that

                                   5   conversation, however, Serrano “misrepresented that the agreed-upon system had been delivered

                                   6   by RingCentral and that all payments—regardless of RingCentral’s performance—were due.” Id.

                                   7   ¶ 29.

                                   8           AmeriSave alleges that these false representations of “progress” continued through March

                                   9   2022, several months after AmeriSave’s termination of the MSA in January 2022. Id. ¶ 31. It was

                                  10   not until April 2023—while preparing for mediation—that AmeriSave alleges that it first

                                  11   “identified information demonstrating that RingCentral had a history of making false

                                  12   representations to customers to induce them into contracts which RingCentral could not carry out,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   thereby forcing clients to pay for services that were never rendered.” Id. Prior to this discovery,

                                  14   “AmeriSave believed RingCentral’s failure to implement the system was attributable solely to

                                  15   delays, technical difficulties, or incompetence, and had no reason to suspect that RingCentral had

                                  16   wrongfully induced AmeriSave into the MSA.” Id. ¶ 32.

                                  17           Because of these alleged misrepresentations, AmeriSave was “forced to return to its

                                  18   original telephony system,” and “spent significant time and resources to ultimately obtain the

                                  19   solution RingCentral had promised in the MSA.” Id. ¶¶ 33–34.

                                  20      2. Procedural History

                                  21           On October 9, 2025, RingCentral filed suit against AmeriSave, alleging a breach of the

                                  22   parties’ written contract. Complaint [Dkt. No. 1]. Later, on November 4, 2025, AmeriSave filed

                                  23   its answer to the complaint, along with its counterclaim against RingCentral. Counterclaim [Dkt.

                                  24   No. 15]. On January 7, 2026, I dismissed AmeriSave’s counterclaim with leave to amend, finding

                                  25   that the counterclaim failed to establish that the delayed discovery rule applied, and that the claims

                                  26   lacked sufficient factual support to survive Rule 9(b). See Minute Entry for Proceedings on

                                  27   January 7, 2026 [Dkt. No. 34].

                                  28           On January 27, 2026, AmeriSave filed an amended counterclaim (the “AC”). See Answer
                                                                                         3
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO             Document 53          Filed 04/29/26      Page 4 of 17




                                   1   to Complaint and Counterclaim [Dkt. No. 39]. On February 10, 2026, RingCentral filed both a

                                   2   motion to dismiss the counterclaim, see Motion to Dismiss Counterclaim (“Dismiss Mot.”) [Dkt.

                                   3   No. 40], and a motion to strike, see Motion to Strike Answer to Complaint (“Strike Mot.”) [Dkt.

                                   4   No. 42]. AmeriSave responded to both motions on February 24, 2026. See Response in

                                   5   Opposition to Motion to Strike (“Strike Oppo.”) [Dkt. No. 44]; Response in Opposition to Motion

                                   6   to Dismiss (“Dismiss Oppo.”) [Dkt. No. 45]. RingCentral replied on March 3, 2026. See Reply in

                                   7   Support of Motion to Dismiss (“Dismiss Repl.”) [Dkt. No. 48]; Reply in Support of Motion to

                                   8   Strike (“Strike Repl.”) [Dkt. No. 49]. I heard oral argument on March 25, 2026.

                                   9                                           LEGAL STANDARD

                                  10   Motion to Dismiss

                                  11       1. Rule 12(b)(6)

                                  12           Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), a district court must dismiss a complaint
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   if it fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6). To survive a

                                  14   Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, the plaintiff must allege “enough facts to state a claim to relief

                                  15   that is plausible on its face.” Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007). A claim is

                                  16   facially plausible when the plaintiff pleads facts that “allows the court to draw the reasonable

                                  17   inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662,

                                  18   678 (2009) (citation omitted). There must be “more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has

                                  19   acted unlawfully.” Id. While courts do not require “heightened fact pleading of specifics,” a

                                  20   plaintiff must allege facts sufficient to “raise a right to relief above the speculative level.”

                                  21   Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555, 570.

                                  22           In deciding whether the plaintiff has stated a claim upon which relief can be granted, the

                                  23   Court accepts the plaintiffs’ allegations as true and “draw[s] all reasonable inferences in favor of

                                  24   the nonmoving party.” Usher v. City of Los Angeles, 828 F.2d 556, 561 (9th Cir. 1987). But the

                                  25   court is not required to accept as true “allegations that are merely conclusory, unwarranted

                                  26   deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.” In re Gilead Scis. Sec. Litig., 536 F.3d 1049,

                                  27   1055 (9th Cir. 2008) (quoting Sprewell v. Golden State Warriors, 266 F.3d 979, 988 (9th Cir.

                                  28   2001), amended on other grounds, 275 F.3d 1187 (9th Cir. 2001)).
                                                                                           4
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO            Document 53          Filed 04/29/26     Page 5 of 17




                                   1          If the court dismisses the complaint, it “should grant leave to amend even if no request to

                                   2   amend the pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading could not possibly be cured

                                   3   by the allegation of other facts.” Doe v. United States, 58 F.3d 494, 497 (9th Cir. 1995). In

                                   4   making this determination, the court should consider factors such as “the presence or absence of

                                   5   undue delay, bad faith, dilatory motive, repeated failure to cure deficiencies by previous

                                   6   amendments, undue prejudice to the opposing party and futility of the proposed amendment.”

                                   7   Moore v. Kayport Package Express, Inc., 885 F.2d 531, 538 (9th Cir. 1989).

                                   8      2. Rule 9(b)

                                   9          Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b) imposes a heightened pleading standard where a

                                  10   complaint alleges fraud or mistake. Under Rule 9(b), to state a claim for fraud, “a party must state

                                  11   with particularity the circumstances constituting fraud,” and the allegations must be “specific

                                  12   enough to give defendants notice of the particular misconduct . . . so that they can defend against
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   the charge and not just deny that they have done anything wrong.” Kearns v. Ford Motor Co., 567

                                  14   F.3d 1120, 1124 (9th Cir. 2009) (citations omitted). “Averments of fraud must be accompanied by

                                  15   ‘the who, what, when, where, and how’ of the misconduct charged.” Vess v. Ciba-Geigy Corp.

                                  16   USA, 317 F.3d 1097, 1106 (9th Cir. 2003) (citation omitted). But “Rule 9(b) requires only that the

                                  17   circumstances of fraud be stated with particularity; other facts may be plead[ed] generally, or in

                                  18   accordance with Rule 8.” United States ex rel. Lee v. Corinthian Colls., 655 F.3d 984, 992 (9th

                                  19   Cir. 2011) (emphasis omitted).

                                  20   Motion to Strike

                                  21          Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(f) allows the court to strike from a pleading an

                                  22   insufficient defense or any redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter. Fed. R. Civ.

                                  23   P. 12(f). “The function of a 12(f) motion to strike is to avoid the expenditure of time and money

                                  24   that must arise from litigating spurious issues by dispensing with those issues prior to trial.”

                                  25   Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., 618 F.3d 970, 973 (9th Cir. 2010) (citation and alteration

                                  26   omitted). Motions to strike “are generally disfavored because the motions may be used as

                                  27   delaying tactics and because of the strong policy favoring resolution on the merits.” Barnes v. AT

                                  28   & T Pension Ben. Plan-Nonbargained Program, 718 F. Supp. 2d 1167, 1170 (N.D. Cal. 2010)
                                                                                          5
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO            Document 53         Filed 04/29/26     Page 6 of 17




                                   1   (Patel, J.) (citation omitted). Such motions should only be granted if “the matter has no logical

                                   2   connection to the controversy at issue and may prejudice one or more of the parties to the suit.”

                                   3   N.Y.C. Emps. Ret. Sys. v. Berry, 667 F. Supp. 2d 1121, 1128 (N.D. Cal. 2009) (Ware, J.) (citation

                                   4   omitted). “Where the moving party cannot adequately demonstrate such prejudice, courts

                                   5   frequently deny motions to strike even though the offending matter literally was within one or

                                   6   more of the categories set forth in Rule 12(f).” Id. (citation and quotation marks omitted).

                                   7   “Ultimately, whether to grant a motion to strike lies within the sound discretion of the district

                                   8   court.” Cruz v. Bank of New York Mellon, No. 12-cv-00846-LHK, 2012 WL 2838957, at *2 (N.D.

                                   9   Cal. July 10, 2012) (Koh, J.) (citing Whittlestone, 618 F.3d at 973).

                                  10                                              DISCUSSION

                                  11   I.     Motion to Dismiss
                                  12          A.      Rule 15
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15 provides the rules for amending complaints, including

                                  14   when amendment is allowed “as a matter of course” or with the court’s approval. Fed. R. Civ. P.

                                  15   15(a). “Once the plaintiff elects to file an amended complaint, the new complaint is the only

                                  16   operative complaint before the district court.” Askins v. U.S. Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 899 F.3d

                                  17   1035, 1043 (9th Cir. 2018).

                                  18          RingCentral argues that the AC is barred under Rule 15 as it contains “impermissible

                                  19   contradiction[s]” compared to the original complaint. See Mot. at 3–4. Unlike the original

                                  20   complaint, which focused only on the fact that “RingCentral disclosed the alleged ‘fundamental

                                  21   limitation’ on October 20, 2021,” the AC now alleges that AmeriSave discovered the allegedly

                                  22   fraudulent conduct in 2023. Id.; see AC ¶ 24. Since it believes October 20, 2021, is the correct

                                  23   date for determining the relevant statute of limitations, RingCentral concludes that the AC

                                  24   “contradicts [AmeriSave’s] earlier factual theory to avoid dismissal.” Id. at 4.

                                  25          Rule 15 notably does not contain any provision prohibiting later-filed complaints from

                                  26   containing “contradictory” statements. Indeed, as the Ninth Circuit has indicated, “[o]nce the

                                  27   plaintiff elects to file an amended complaint, the new complaint is the only operative complaint

                                  28   before the district court.” Askins, 899 F.3d at 1043. While RingCentral may certainly attack
                                                                                         6
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO             Document 53         Filed 04/29/26     Page 7 of 17




                                   1   AmeriSave’s theory for why its AC meets the statute of limitations, AmeriSave did not violate

                                   2   Rule 15 by merely providing new facts that Ring Central views as “contradictory.” I decline to

                                   3   dismiss the AC under Rule 15.

                                   4          B.      Statute of Limitations
                                   5                  1.      Counts One, Two, and Three – Fraud Claims
                                   6          Under California law, fraudulent misrepresentation, fraud in the inducement, and non-

                                   7   professional negligent misrepresentation claims are subject to a three-year statute of limitations,

                                   8   see CAL. CIV. PROC. CODE § 338(d), whereas negligent misrepresentation claims made by

                                   9   professionals are subject to a two-year statute of limitations, see id. § 339(1). While the parties

                                  10   disagree as to when the statute of limitations tolled in this case, both agree that the sufficiency of

                                  11   the AC depends on whether the delayed discovery rule can be invoked.

                                  12          To invoke the delayed discovery rule, the pleading party “must specifically plead facts to
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   show (1) the time and manner of discovery and (2) the inability to have made earlier discovery

                                  14   despite reasonable diligence.” Fox v. Ethicon Endo-Surgery, Inc., 35 Cal. 4th 797, 808 (2005)

                                  15   (cleaned up). “In assessing the sufficiency of the allegations of delayed discovery, the court

                                  16   places the burden on the plaintiff to show diligence; conclusory allegations will not withstand” a

                                  17   motion to dismiss. See id. (internal quotations omitted). But the delayed discovery rule “only

                                  18   delays accrual until the plaintiff has, or should have, inquiry notice of the cause of action.” Id. at

                                  19   807. A plaintiff has inquiry notice “when [she] suspects or should suspect that her injury was

                                  20   caused by wrongdoing, that someone has done something wrong to her.” Jolly v. Eli Lilly & Co.,

                                  21   44 Cal. 3d 1103, 1110 (1988) (emphasis added). “[P]laintiffs are required to conduct a reasonable

                                  22   investigation after becoming aware of an injury, and are charged with knowledge of the

                                  23   information that would have been revealed by such an investigation.” Fox, 35 Cal. 4th at 808.

                                  24   “The question when a plaintiff actually discovered or reasonably should have discovered the facts

                                  25   for purposes of the delayed discovery rule is a question of fact unless the evidence can support

                                  26   only one reasonable conclusion.” Ovando v. Cnty. of L.A., 159 Cal. App. 4th 42, 61 (2008).

                                  27          RingCentral argues that AmeriSave discovered the purported fraud on October 20, 2021,

                                  28   when “RingCentral’s Senior Manager of Professional Services, Stewart Goldfarb, stated that
                                                                                          7
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO            Document 53         Filed 04/29/26    Page 8 of 17




                                   1   RingCentral ‘couldn’t deliver the calls at a pace necessary to achieve AmeriSave’s business

                                   2   objectives,’ noting that the implementation RingCentral had originally promised was not able to

                                   3   be implemented due to a ‘fundamental limitation.’” AC ¶ 24; see Mot. at 4–7. AmeriSave, in

                                   4   response, asserts that the AC raises additional facts showing that the delayed discovery rule

                                   5   applies. See Oppo. at 6–8. It points out that the AC alleges the parties were in communication for

                                   6   months after discovering the “fundamental limitation,” as RingCentral’s “senior executives

                                   7   [expressed a] commit[ment] to delivering a system to AmeriSave and working toward an amicable

                                   8   resolution for the Parties.” AC ¶ 28. RingCentral then “continued to falsely represent that

                                   9   progress was being made on the system through March 2022, several months after AmeriSave’s

                                  10   termination of the MSA in January 2022.” Id. ¶ 30. It was not until 2023, when preparing for

                                  11   mediation, that AmeriSave “identified information demonstrating that RingCentral had a history

                                  12   of making false representations to customers to induce them into contracts which RingCentral
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   could not carry out, thereby forcing clients to pay for services that were never rendered.” Id. ¶ 31.

                                  14   The AC then concludes by noting that “[p]rior to discovering this information in 2023, AmeriSave

                                  15   believed RingCentral’s failure to implement the system was attributable solely to delays, technical

                                  16   difficulties, or incompetence, and had no reason to suspect that RingCentral had wrongfully

                                  17   induced AmeriSave into the MSA.” Id. ¶ 32.

                                  18          AmeriSave has not pleaded that its fraud-based claims can survive under the delayed

                                  19   discovery rule. Notably, AmeriSave concedes that it discovered the “fundamental limitation”—

                                  20   that RingCentral could not deliver its system—on October 20, 2021, when Goldfarb indicated it

                                  21   could not meet its contractual promises. AC ¶ 24. A plaintiff may be placed on “inquiry notice”

                                  22   of its fraud claims when they “bec[o]me aware” of their injury. See Platt Elec. Supply, Inc. v.

                                  23   EOFF Elec., Inc., 522 F.3d 1049, 1055 (9th Cir. 2008) (finding plaintiff was on inquiry notice

                                  24   upon learning defects in 1999, despite claiming later discovery of wrongdoing in 2001). Without

                                  25   more facts, it appears that AmeriSave “should have been suspicious” that RingCentral negligently

                                  26   or fraudulently represented its capacity to deliver a functional system as soon as October 20, 2021,

                                  27   when RingCentral acknowledged its “fundamental limitation.” See id.; AC ¶ 24. As AmeriSave

                                  28   expressly concedes in its complaint, if “its telephones do not work properly, [it] simply cannot
                                                                                         8
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO             Document 53        Filed 04/29/26      Page 9 of 17




                                   1   conduct its business.” AC ¶ 10. Given the “extensive [potential] legal and economic

                                   2   repercussions” produced by the “fundamental limitation,” AmeriSave had “reason to at least

                                   3   suspect that a type of wrongdoing ha[d] injured [it].” Id. ¶ 24; Platt, 522 F.3d at 1055–56 (quoting

                                   4   V.C. v. L.A. Unified Sch. Dist., 139 Cal. App. 4th 499, 516 (2006)). Because “it is the discovery of

                                   5   facts, not their legal significance, that starts the statute,” AmeriSave cannot rely on its findings

                                   6   during mediation preparation in 2023 to revive its fraud-based claims. Jolly, 44 Cal. 3d at 1113

                                   7   (citation omitted, emphasis added). RingCentral’s motion to dismiss AmeriSave’s fraud claims as

                                   8   tolled by the statute of limitations is GRANTED.

                                   9                  2.      Contract Claims
                                  10          Breach of contract claims under California law are subject to a four-year statute of

                                  11   limitations for written contracts, see CAL. CIV. PROC. CODE § 337, and two years for oral contracts,

                                  12   see id. at 339(1), while promissory estoppel claims are subject to a two-year statute of limitations,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   see id.1 Both parties agree that the statute of limitations for a contract claim accrues at the time of

                                  14   breach. See McCaskey v. Cal. State Auto. Ass’n, 189 Cal. App. 4th 947, 959 (2010). But a breach

                                  15   must be “actually discharged” for the statute of limitations to begin running. See id.

                                  16          RingCentral argues that the purported breach of contract occurred when AmeriSave

                                  17   learned of the “fundamental limitation” affecting its ability to effectuate the MSA. See Mot. at 4–

                                  18   7; AC ¶ 24. AmeriSave, in turn, asserts that the breach did not occur until January 31, 2022, when

                                  19   AmeriSave repudiated the contract. See Oppo. at 9; AC ¶ 30. AmeriSave has the stronger

                                  20   argument at this stage of litigation. While the AC identifies the October 20, 2021 “fundamental

                                  21   limitation” conversation as constituting a “material breach,” see AC ¶ 2, it also indicates that the

                                  22   breach of contract was “actually discharged” on January 31, 2022, when “AmeriSave . . .

                                  23   terminat[ed] the MSA,” see id. ¶ 30; McCaskey, 189 Cal. App. 4th at 959. Construing the breach

                                  24

                                  25   1
                                        AmeriSave’s breach of contract claim concerns alleged violations of the parties’ MSA. See AC
                                  26   ¶¶ 68–73. While the AC does not indicate whether the MSA was an oral or written contract,
                                       RingCentral’s request for judicial notice confirms that the agreement was written. See Request for
                                  27   Judicial Notice (“RJN”) [Dkt. No. 41] Ex. A Master Services Agreement (“MSA”). Accordingly,
                                       AmeriSave’s breach of contract claim is subject to a four-year statute of limitations. CAL. CIV.
                                  28
                                       PROC. CODE § 339(1).
                                                                                        9
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO            Document 53           Filed 04/29/26    Page 10 of 17




                                   1   to occur in January 2022, therefore, AmeriSave’s breach of contract claim, filed on October 9,

                                   2   2025, is within the four-year statute of limitations. But the promissory estoppel claim, with only a

                                   3   two-year statute of limitations, is untimely. I accordingly GRANT RingCentral’s motion to

                                   4   dismiss the promissory estoppel claim but DENY it as to the breach of contract claim.

                                   5          C.      Failure to State a Claim – Rules 9(b) and 12(b)(6)
                                   6                  1.      Counts One and Three – Fraudulent Misrepresentation and Negligent
                                                              Misrepresentation
                                   7
                                              Both the first and second count of AmeriSave’s AC sound in fraud. “The elements of
                                   8
                                       fraudulent misrepresentation are the same as the elements for a fraud claim.” Bankers Life & Cas.
                                   9
                                       Co. v. Mallin, 808 F. Supp. 3d 1062, 1076 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (Lin, J.) (citing Yamauchi v.
                                  10
                                       Cotterman, 84 F. Supp. 3d 993, 1018 (N.D. Cal. 2015)).
                                  11
                                              To state a claim for fraudulent misrepresentation, a plaintiff must show “(1) a
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       misrepresentation or omission of a fact that should have been disclosed; (2) knowledge of falsity;
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       (3) intent to induce reliance; (4) justifiable reliance; and (5) resulting damage.” Id.; see Lazar v.
                                  14
                                       Superior Court, 12 Cal. 4th 631, 638 (1996). Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b), “[i]n
                                  15
                                       alleging fraud or mistake, a party must state with particularity the circumstances constituting fraud
                                  16
                                       or mistake.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b). In other words, to plausibly allege a claim for fraudulent
                                  17
                                       misrepresentation, AmeriSave must establish “the who, what, when, where, and how” of the
                                  18
                                       misconduct charged. Vess, 317 F.3d at 1106.
                                  19
                                              Similarly, to establish a claim for negligent misrepresentation, a plaintiff must show that
                                  20
                                       the defendant “(1) made a misrepresentation of a past or existing material fact, (2) without
                                  21
                                       reasonable ground for believing it to be true, (3) with intent to induce another’s reliance on the fact
                                  22
                                       misrepresented, (4) justifiable reliance on the misrepresentation, and (5) resulting damage.”
                                  23
                                       Maeda v. Pinnacle Foods Inc., 390 F. Supp. 3d 1231, 1257 (D. Haw. 2019) (collecting cases).
                                  24
                                       While the Ninth Circuit has “not yet decided whether Rule 9(b)’s pleading standard applies to a
                                  25
                                       claim for negligent misrepresentation, . . . most district courts in California hold that it does.”
                                  26
                                       Villegas v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., No. 12-cv-02004 LB, 2012 WL 4097747, at *7 (N.D. Cal.
                                  27
                                       Sept. 17, 2012) (Beeler, M.J.). AmeriSave does not appear to argue that it must only meet the
                                  28
                                                                                          10
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO           Document 53          Filed 04/29/26   Page 11 of 17




                                   1   Rule 8 pleading standard for purposes of resolving the present motion. I therefore assume Rule

                                   2   9(b) applies to AmeriSave’s negligent misrepresentation claim.

                                   3          RingCentral argues that AmeriSave failed to adequately plead either of its fraud claims, as

                                   4   the AC “does not identify the precise statements, by which speaker, on what date(s), in what

                                   5   medium, nor facts showing contemporaneous falsity or scienter.” Mot. at 10. I agree. The AC

                                   6   alleges that during two meetings between RingCentral and AmeriSave on March 23, 2021, and

                                   7   April 2, 2021, “RingCentral, through its executives, represented that it could create a custom,

                                   8   cloud-based communication platform system for AmeriSave that would resolve [its] call quality

                                   9   and scalability issues.” AC ¶¶ 14, 16. Despite this, RingCentral was unable to complete the

                                  10   platform and instead “attempt[ed] to conceal [its] inability to implement the agreed-upon system.”

                                  11   Id. ¶¶ 20, 23. AmeriSave then alleges numerous instances between October 2021 and March 2022

                                  12   where RingCentral “falsely represent[ed] that progress was being made on the system.” See id. ¶¶
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   24–30. But it was not until “early 2023, during AmeriSave’s preparations for an April 2023

                                  14   mediation and its aftermath, [that] it identified information demonstrating that RingCentral had a

                                  15   history of making false representations to customers to induce them into contracts which

                                  16   RingCentral could not carry out, thereby forcing clients to pay for services that were never

                                  17   rendered.” Id. ¶ 31.

                                  18          These facts, taken together, are not sufficient to establish the “who, what, when, where,

                                  19   and how” of RingCentral’s purportedly fraudulent misconduct. Vess, 317 F.3d at 1106.

                                  20   Importantly, the AC does not identify with particularity what “information demonstrate[ed] . . .

                                  21   RingCentral had a history of making false representations” when preparing for its April 2023

                                  22   mediation. AC ¶ 31. Nor does AmeriSave explain what such “false representations” were made

                                  23   in those other contracts. See id. Its “barebone assertions do not satisfy the heightened pleading

                                  24   requirements of Rule 9(b).” Zearfoss v. Rubbermaid, Inc., No. 2:18-cv-06392-AB (ASx), 2018

                                  25   WL 8731935, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Dec. 21, 2018).

                                  26                  2.      Counts Four and Five – Breach of Contract and Promissory Estoppel
                                  27          RingCentral also moves to dismiss AmeriSave’s breach of contract and promissory

                                  28   estoppel claims under Rule 12(b)(6). Under California law, to plead a breach of contract claim, a
                                                                                        11
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO            Document 53        Filed 04/29/26      Page 12 of 17




                                   1   party must allege four elements: “[1] that a contract exists between the parties, [2] that the plaintiff

                                   2   performed his contractual duties or was excused from nonperformance, [3] that the defendant

                                   3   breached those contractual duties, and [4] that plaintiff’s damages were a result of the breach.”

                                   4   Boland, Inc. v. Rolf C. Hagen (USA) Corp., 685 F. Supp. 2d 1094, 1101 (E.D. Cal. 2010) (citing

                                   5   Reichert v. Gen. Ins. Co., 68 Cal. 2d 822, 830 (1968)). Similarly, for promissory estoppel claims,

                                   6   a plaintiff must allege “(1) a promise clear and unambiguous in its terms; (2) reliance by the party

                                   7   to whom the promise is made; (3) the reliance must be both reasonable and foreseeable; and (4)

                                   8   the party asserting the estoppel must be injured by his reliance.” Granadino v. Wells Fargo Bank,

                                   9   N.A., 236 Cal. App. 4th 411, 416 (2015) (cleaned up).

                                  10          With respect to AmeriSave’s breach of contract claim, RingCentral maintains that the AC

                                  11   “does not allege that [it] failed to perform any concrete, promised obligation under the integrated

                                  12   MSA (including Attachments and Order Forms), as opposed to failing to meet evolving, extra-
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   contractual preferences.” Mot. at 11. I disagree. AmeriSave need not “allege the specific terms

                                  14   of the contract” under Rule 8, so long as “adequate specific facts” are provided to allege breach of

                                  15   contract. Westway World Travel v. AMR Corp., 182 F. Supp. 2d 952, 963 (C.D. Cal. 2001). That

                                  16   is met here. As AmeriSave notes in its Opposition, the AC “alleges the existence of the MSA and

                                  17   attached agreements; alleges that AmeriSave was excused from performance of its obligations due

                                  18   to RingCentral’s failure to implement the system; alleges that RingCentral promised to implement

                                  19   a custom, cloud-based telephony system and failed to do so; and alleges damages resulting from

                                  20   that failure.” Oppo. at 13; see AC ¶¶ 19–22, 34, 68–73. Because AmeriSave establishes each

                                  21   element of a breach of contract claim with sufficient particularity, I decline to dismiss this claim.2

                                  22

                                  24   2
                                         Because I find AmeriSave’s promissory estoppel claim barred by the statute of limitations, I
                                  25   decline to address RingCentral’s argument that the promissory estoppel claim must be dismissed
                                       because “promissory estoppel claims are generally unavailable where the parties have entered into
                                  26   a contract supported by consideration.” Mot. at 12. Even so, I will note that to dismiss the
                                       promissory estoppel claim on these grounds would be a merits judgment. AmeriSave may allege a
                                  27   duplicative breach of contract and promissory estoppel claim in its complaint. See Fed. R. Civ. P.
                                       8(d)(3) (allowing “[a] party [to] state as many separate claims or defenses as it has, regardless of
                                  28   consistency”); Herbalife Int’l of Am., Inc. v. E. Computer Exch., Inc., 723 F. Supp. 3d 888, 911
                                       (C.D. Cal. 2024) (indicating that promissory is an alternative claim to a breach of contract).

                                              D.      Economic Loss Rule
                                   1
                                              RingCentral also argues that the economic loss rule provides an independent basis for
                                   2
                                       dismissal. “The economic loss rule limits a party to a contract ‘to recover[ing] in contract for
                                   3
                                       purely economic loss due to disappointed expectations,’ rather than in tort, ‘unless he can
                                   4
                                       demonstrate harm above and beyond a broken contractual promise.’” Rattagan v. Uber Techs.,
                                   5
                                       Inc., 19 F.4th 1188, 1191 (9th Cir. 2021) (quoting Robinson Helicopter Co. v. Dana Corp., 34 Cal.
                                   6
                                       4th 979, 988 (2004)). “Stated differently, a party to a contract generally cannot recover for pure
                                   7
                                       economic loss—i.e., damages that are solely monetary—that resulted from a breach of contract
                                   8
                                       unless he can show a violation of some independent duty arising in tort.” Id. This rule is meant to
                                   9
                                       “prevent[] the law of contract and the law of tort from dissolving one into the other.” Robinson,
                                  10
                                       34 Cal. 4th at 988 (internal quotation omitted).
                                  11
                                              RingCentral maintains that the AC alleges damages that are “purely economic and . . . arise
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       solely from disappointed contractual expectation.” Mot. at 12. Because AmeriSave purportedly
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       “alleges no injury independent of disappointed performance, all tort claims are barred” by the
                                  14
                                       economic loss rule. Id. While AmeriSave acknowledges the economic loss rule, it believes the
                                  15
                                       rule “does not apply where the defendant’s conduct violates an independent tort duty.” Oppo. at
                                  16
                                       14; see Robinson Helicopter, 34 Cal. 4th at 998; Erlich v. Menezes, 21 Cal. 4th 543, 554 (1999).
                                  17
                                       Because the AC “alleges that RingCentral made affirmative, materially false statements and
                                  18
                                       concealed critical limitations before and after execution of the MSA, inducing AmeriSave to enter
                                  19
                                       into and continue performing under the MSA,” AmeriSave concludes that an independent tort of
                                  20
                                       fraud is actionable. Oppo. at 15.
                                  21
                                              To support its argument, AmeriSave cites to many cases it believes show that California
                                  22
                                       courts allow tort recovery for these types of intentional misconduct. Id. at 14–15 (citing Robinson
                                  23
                                       Helicopter, 34 Cal. 4th at 991–92); Lou v. Am. Honda Motor Co., No. 16-cv-04384-JST, 2022 WL
                                  24
                                       18539358, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 26, 2022) (Tigar, J.); Weisberg v. Takeda Pharm. Co. Ltd., No.
                                  25
                                       CV 18-784 PA (JCx), 2018 WL 6219879, at *5 (C.D. Cal. May 7, 2018)). In each of those cases,
                                  26
                                       the courts found intentional misrepresentations rooted outside the scope of the contract, such as
                                  27
                                       false certificates of conformance about a product’s safety standards. See Robinson Helicopter, 34
                                  28
                                                                                          13

                                   1   Cal. 4th at 991–92.

                                   2          AmeriSave’s fraud claims appear to saddle the line between tort and contract. But

                                   3   construing all facts in favor of the nonmoving party, AmeriSave meets its burden to survive the

                                   4   economic loss rule. The AC alleges that RingCentral “knew [in March and April 2021] that it

                                   5   could not create a custom, cloud-based communication platform system, particularly in light of

                                   6   fundamental limitations in its capabilities of which it was aware of before entering into the MSA.”

                                   7   AC ¶ 38. Nonetheless, RingCentral “promised timely delivery of its products and services,

                                   8   knowing it had no capacity to fulfill that promise, to induce AmeriSave to enter into the MSA.”

                                   9   Id. ¶ 41. AmeriSave, “with no prior experience in the relevant market,” ultimately relied on

                                  10   RingCentral’s “expertise and assurances.” Id. ¶¶ 37, 42. While the parties memorialized their

                                  11   ultimate agreement via contract, the underlying claim at issue here—RingCentral’s prior claims

                                  12   that it could fulfill the contract, despite its knowledge otherwise—sound in tort. RingCentral’s
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   motion to dismiss on the economic loss rule is accordingly DENIED.

                                  14          E.      Integration Clause
                                  15          Finally, RingCentral contends that the MSA’s integration clause bars any extra-contractual

                                  16   arguments made by AmeriSave. See Mot. at 13–15. The MSA contains an express integration

                                  17   clause that reads:

                                  18                  J. Entire Agreement. The Agreement, together with any exhibits,
                                                      Order Forms, Use Policies, Data Processing Addendum and
                                  19                  Attachments, each of which is expressly incorporated into this
                                                      Agreement with this reference, constitutes the entire agreement
                                  20                  between the Parties and supersedes and replaces any and all prior or
                                                      contemporaneous understandings, proposals, representations,
                                  21                  marketing materials, statements, or agreements, whether oral, written,
                                                      or otherwise, regarding such subject.
                                  22
                                       RJN MSA. RingCentral argues that the AC rests “entirely on pre-contract sales demonstrations,
                                  23
                                       capability pitches, and timing assurances – the precise ‘representations’ and ‘marketing materials’
                                  24
                                       the integration clause excludes.” Mot. at 13. In its view, therefore, the integration clause provides
                                  25
                                       an additional basis for dismissal. See id.
                                  26
                                              RingCentral is mistaken. Under Section 1856(g) of the California Civil Code, the parole
                                  27
                                       evidence rule “does not exclude other evidence of the circumstances under which the agreement
                                  28
                                                                                        14
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08694-WHO           Document 53           Filed 04/29/26    Page 15 of 17




                                   1   was made or to which it relates . . . or to explain an extrinsic ambiguity or otherwise interpret the

                                   2   terms of the agreement, or to establish illegality or fraud.” CAL. CIV. PROC. CODE § 1856(g)

                                   3   (emphasis added). In other words, California law explicitly permits parties to introduce extrinsic

                                   4   evidence to prove fraud, notwithstanding any integration or merger clauses in the parties’

                                   5   contracts. While the AC’s fraud claims are currently deficient, the integration clause alone does

                                   6   not provide an independent basis for dismissal. RingCentral’s motion to dismiss is DENIED on

                                   7   this ground.

                                   8   II.    MOTION TO STRIKE
                                   9          RingCentral seeks to strike from the AC (1) requests for punitive damages, (2) allegations

                                  10   referencing mediation proceedings or settlement communications, (3) allegations of RingCentral’s

                                  11   “pattern” or “history” of misconduct toward other customers, and (4) requests for attorneys’ fees.

                                  12   Each request is DENIED.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          A.      Punitive Damages
                                  14          California Civil Code section 3294 governs whether a party may seek punitive damages for

                                  15   a noncontractual breach of obligation. See CAL. CIV. CODE § 3294. Under this section, a plaintiff

                                  16   may recover punitive damages by showing, by “clear and convincing evidence,” that the other

                                  17   party “has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice.” Id. § 3294(a). RingCentral asserts that the

                                  18   AC does not plead “facts showing conduct sufficiently egregious to justify punishment” via

                                  19   punitive damages. Strike Mot. at 1. It also maintains that AmeriSave fails to satisfy Section

                                  20   3294(b), which requires a party alleging fraud by a corporation to plead that an “officer, director,

                                  21   or managing agent” had “advance knowledge” of, or consciously disregarded, authorized, or

                                  22   ratified, an “act of oppression, fraud, or malice.” CAL. CIV. CODE § 3294(b).

                                  23          I agree with RingCentral that the AC currently lacks sufficient allegations to sustain a

                                  24   claim for punitive damages under Section 3294. As discussed above, the AC does not sufficiently

                                  25   allege RingCentral’s fraudulent behavior. Nor does it plead specific allegations tying any alleged

                                  26   fraud to a director or other qualifying corporate officer. But it is plausible that AmeriSave could

                                  27   fix this issue by amending its counterclaim. I therefore DENY RingCentral’s motion as

                                  28   premature.

                                       Rule 408’s scope. It is unclear whether AmeriSave’s references to RingCentral’s “prior pattern of

                                                 C.     Allegations of “Pattern” of Misconduct

                                                 Next, RingCentral argues that AmeriSave “repeatedly alleges an unspecified ‘pattern’ or
                                  21
                                       ‘history’ of misconduct toward unidentified customers,” which it contends led to the discovery of
                                  22
                                       the alleged fraud. Strike Mot. at 5. RingCentral asserts that such allegations are inadmissible

                                       under FRE 404 as improper character evidence. See id.

                                                 RingCentral’s argument is not persuasive. First, AmeriSave does not appear to rely on an

                                       alleged pattern to prove RingCentral’s propensity to mistreat customers; rather, it invokes such
                                  26
                                       allegations to show RingCentral’s absence of mistake, intent, and knowledge in connection with

                                   3   misconduct? AmeriSave must add more facts to its amended counterclaim for these statements to

                                   4   not be struck.

                                   5          D.        Attorneys’ Fees
                                   6          Finally, RingCentral moves to strike AmeriSave’s request for attorneys’ fees on the ground

                                   7   that the AC lacks any specific statutory or contractual basis for recovery. Strike Mot. at 5. I

                                   8   DENY this request. A motion to strike is proper if the matter to be stricken is “redundant,

                                   9   immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(f). AmeriSave’s request for attorney’s

                                  10   fees does not meet any of those standards. And even if the request currently lacks legal support,

                                  11   Rule 12(f) is not meant to test the legal sufficiency of remedies. This issue is best addressed later

                                  12   as this case progresses.

 United States District Court

                                  16   RingCentral’s motion to strike is DENIED. AmeriSave shall have twenty-one (21) days from the

                                  17   date of this Order to submit a Second Amended Counterclaim.
